latin.etymology: From fūr, fūris (thief), with instrumental suffix -tim. The root traces to PIE *bʰor- (to carry away). Related to Greek φώρ (phṓr, thief).
latin.literary_context: Catullus uses fūrtim in Poem 68 to describe secret stolen moments of love: fūrtīvā vēnit flāmine mīlītiae. Ovid employs it frequently in the Amores and Metamorphoses for clandestine affairs and divine disguises.
latin.usage_example: Fūrtim in cubiculum dominī intrāvit servus. — The slave entered the master's chamber stealthily.
latin.did_you_know: The adverb fūrtim shares its root with the English words furtive and ferret (originally a thief-animal used for hunting). Roman love poets favored it for describing illicit rendezvous, making it a hallmark of elegiac vocabulary.

greek.forms: ἀναίδεια, ἀναιδείας, ἀναιδείᾳ, ἀναίδειαν (sg.); ἀναίδειαι, ἀναιδειῶν, ἀναιδείαις, ἀναιδείας (pl.)
greek.etymology: From ἀν- (privative 'not') + αἰδώς (shame, reverence, respect). The alpha-privative negates the sense of proper shame or modesty that characterizes civilized behavior.
greek.literary_context: Plato uses ἀναίδεια extensively in the Republic to describe the shameless audacity of the democratic man who acknowledges no hierarchy of values, treating all desires as equal. Thucydides employs it to characterize the brutal frankness of the Athenians at Melos.
greek.usage_example: τῆς ἀναιδείας ἕνεκα οὐδένα αἰδοῦνται. — On account of their shamelessness they respect no one.
greek.did_you_know: While ἀναίδεια denotes the absence of αἰδώς (shame or reverence), ancient Greek culture saw αἰδώς as essential to social order; thus ἀναίδεια represented not mere boldness but a dangerous dissolution of the moral fabric binding the community.

french.meaning: a flourish of trumpets; a brass band; ostentatious display
french.etymology: From Spanish fanfarria or Italian fanfara, probably onomatopoetic in origin, imitating the sound of trumpets. Attested in French from the 16th century.
french.literary_context: Rimbaud uses the word in "Les Illuminations" to evoke the clash of modern spectacle and sensory overload, particularly in pieces like "Parade" where fanfares announce the grotesque circus of contemporary life.
french.usage_example: Les fanfares éclatent sous les fenêtres du palais. — The trumpet flourishes ring out beneath the palace windows.
french.did_you_know: In 17th-century French theater, a fanfare signaled the arrival of royalty or marked a ceremonial moment; Molière's troupes would have heard such flourishes at court performances before Louis XIV.

german.forms: die Grübelei, gen. der Grübelei, pl. die Grübeleien
german.etymology: From the verb grübeln (to brood, to ponder obsessively), itself from Middle High German grübelen, related to Grube (pit, grave), suggesting a digging or delving into thought. The suffix -ei forms abstract nouns denoting continuous or excessive action.
german.literary_context: Schopenhauer uses the concept extensively in Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung, warning against sterile intellectual rumination that deepens suffering rather than alleviating it. Kafka's diaries are filled with references to his own Grübelei as a source of creative paralysis.
german.usage_example: Seine endlose Grübelei über den Sinn des Lebens führte ihn nur tiefer in die Verzweiflung. — His endless brooding over the meaning of life led him only deeper into despair.
german.did_you_know: Schopenhauer distinguished between productive reflection (Nachdenken) and destructive Grübelei, arguing that the latter arises from an inability to accept the will's fundamental nature and leads only to neurasthenia.

oldenglish.forms: nom. wælstōw, acc. wælstōwe, gen. wælstōwe, dat. wælstōwe; plural wælstōwa/wælstōwe
oldenglish.etymology: Compound of wæl (slaughter, carnage) + stōw (place, site). The first element derives from Proto-Germanic *walą (those slain in battle), cognate with Old Norse valr. The second element stōw (place) gives Modern English 'stow' and appears in place names.
oldenglish.literary_context: This word appears prominently in Beowulf (line 2051) where the poet describes ancient battlefields, and in the Battle of Brunanburh from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, where the narrator recounts the devastating battlefield left after the English victory over Norse and Scottish forces in 937 CE.
oldenglish.usage_example: Hēr lāg secg monig / gārum āgetēd, guma norþerna / ofer scield scoten, swilce Scittisc ēac, / wērig, wīges sæd on þām wælstōwe. — Here lay many a warrior, destroyed by spears, northern men shot over their shields, likewise Scottish too, weary, sated with battle, on that slaughter-place.
oldenglish.did_you_know: The compound wælstōw reflects the Germanic poetic tradition of battlefield kennings; its component wæl is related to Valhalla (Old Norse Valhǫll, literally 'hall of the slain'), showing the shared cultural concept of the honored dead across Germanic peoples.
